en: The first chapter, on the inclusion [of other means] within the valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa),
whose stainless light of wisdom devours the entire cycle of the world.
Or, in order to accomplish the welfare of sentient beings, there is another who has arisen, who is not incapable and is stainless (akalaṅkaḥ).
Having bowed to him, who is incomparable, whose speech is gentle, who is not dejected, and who is well-disposed toward the fulfillment of his own purpose; Ms. having bowed to him.
Whether it be perception or inference— by whom this has been declared, he is the peerless lord of rivers (the ocean),
not one who is dejected.
Perception and inference are indeed the only means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
because the convergence of multiple means of cognition is impossible and because there is a correspondence with only two types of objects of cognition (*prameya*);
for verbal testimony and other such means are merely forms of error, being otherwise than those two.
Because it lacks the defining characteristics of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), that which exists externally is a pseudo-means of cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*).

A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not a mere appearance of validity established by a stream of error; rather, if validity is somehow established, then because it possesses the characteristics of inference (*anumāna*), it is not a separate means of cognition. For a means of cognition is that which functions as direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*). In its absence, [inference] is merely an indicator of that [direct perception], owing to the grace of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) therein. That alone is a means of valid cognition which makes known the existence of its own object; otherwise, it would lack validity due to being a cognition of doubt or error. And that which is directly apprehended is precisely what exists, since it is established that "existence" (*sattā*) is nothing other than apprehension itself.
In that case, there is neither doubt nor error, because those two are necessarily restricted to what is not being perceived;
therefore, that which is perceived exists.
The absence of valid cognition is non-deviation by virtue of clarity.
Doubt, error, and lack of awakening constitute non-validity;

and where there is certainty through the obstruction of perception—characterized by direct realization—that other [means] does not exist, such is the rule. Therefore, there are only two means of valid cognition.
The summary of the meaning is this: because presumption (*arthāpatti*) and the other [means of knowledge] lack such a nature, they are not valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Now, if it is argued that even in the absence of such a mode [of existence], it is designated as "existing" simply due to its connection with being (*sattā*), that is incorrect:
for how can there be a comprehension of a connection with being for that which lacks perceptibility?
For that which possesses the state of being perceivable, the further connection with existence is redundant;
otherwise, why is the connection with existence not likewise asserted for things such as the horn of a donkey?
Since things such as echoes and horns are not real entities, one should not approach them [as such]; if they were real entities, what then would be the point?
Furthermore, the reality of that which is perceived cannot be divorced from its apprehension.
If it is produced without apprehension,
then that very thing is its substantiality; what need is there for another?
Therefore, the apprehensibility of an entity is a semblance of perception;
that which is other than this is the cause of the semblance of perception.
These two types of valid cognition arise solely from inference preceded by perception;
otherwise, cognition would not be non-erroneous,
and there exists no cognition distinct from the forms of perception and memory.
If every cognition that does not exist as something distinct [from its object] and every unrelated memory were valid, then all cognition would be valid knowledge (*pramā*).
If that which was previously unrelated becomes related, then it is perceived there, and in that place, it is the object of inference.
If that universal form is also understood from a word,
then that [word] too has attained the status of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), for it is indeed just like inference.
That [other] means of valid cognition is likewise [included within these]; therefore, inference, analogy, presumptive testimony, and so forth are not distinct from these two means of valid cognition.
Therefore,

it is logical that even sound and other [sensory objects] have cognition; since there is cognition of an object beyond the senses, its cognition must arise from inference alone— this is an extreme rashness.
O lady of extreme daring, act accordingly; always direct your mind toward some state of being, and never toward the cultivation of nothingness.
Ms.
[indicates] a slight degree of esteem.
Without this new meaning, linguistic usage is not established;
nor is there any means for attaining heaven and so forth without the meaning of Vedic sentences.
Therefore, there is no lack of authority in this [scripture] for those who partake in the fruits such as heaven.
Furthermore, O lady, this other world is to be established by means of inference.
No logical reason for this has been established anywhere; for even if another world were proven, how could there be a restriction on the results of actions?
Therefore, scripture alone is accepted [as the authority]; if that exists, inference is useless.
Therefore, the next world must necessarily be accepted as established by scripture; for it is unestablished through perception, as is its connection with that [scripture].
Therefore, from scripture, there is the cognition of everything pertaining to the connection with the afterlife.
Therefore, it is understood that all [means of knowledge] such as analogy (upamāna) and the rest do not possess the characteristics of inference (anumāna).
Therefore, if there were the existence of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could it be said that "there are only two"?
[To this, it is replied: another means of valid cognition, namely verbal testimony (*śabda*), is stated to be distinct from inference (*anumāna*).
Ms.

Verbal testimony is described as a means of valid cognition distinct from inference; it expresses its own object through the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), like [the mark] "being produced" and so forth. If that were not the case, the connection [of words] with the other world would not be established.
And it will be stated later that validity [belongs] to the intention to speak; however,
worldly linguistic usage always concerns the meaning of a sentence, whereas for people there is never linguistic usage by means of a single word alone.
For one who knows yoga does not [perceive] the novelty of creation in either the sentence or its meaning;
indeed, all [is known].
Therefore, how indeed can it be maintained that the word has exclusion (*apoha*) as its object?
Furthermore, if it is argued that the relationship between the word and its referent is well-established,
then why is that [relationship] not simply an inference once the connection has been grasped?

That is incorrect; for even a word is not accepted as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since it does not differ from a mere reminder (*smāraka*) due to the absence of any additional [informative] content.
Furthermore, some maintain that a word always denotes a meaning already connected [with others].

If it were to express a contrary meaning, how could there be a subsequent connection? How could there be the abandonment of what has already been accepted? If there is abandonment, that word is useless;
for if it expresses a non-connected meaning, it is like the sentence "ten pomegranates."
If it is argued that linguistic usage cannot occur because there is no perceived relationship [between word and object], even so,
if a relationship exists later on, then let the sentence itself be the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) even in that case where the meaning is not [previously] connected.
The fact that the relationship [between word and meaning] has not been apprehended there was already established previously;
therefore, inference is not capable of functioning between a sentence and its sentence-meaning. For every word-meaning here is thus connected with other word-meanings.
This sentence-meaning is indeed like a divine cloth (devakambala); how else could it be?

Now, if it is argued that comprehension here depends on context— otherwise there would be no context for the word— then how could such a fault be stated by one who knows the means of valid cognition regarding the connection with another word within a uniform context?
How can there be a restricted cognition [of an object] based on another word that has the same sound?
Furthermore, the relationship between a word and its meaning is not characterized by "origination from that" (tadutpatti) and so forth;
rather, in that case, only the relationship of signifier and signified (vācyavācaka) is accepted.
Nor does it possess the status of a logical reason (*hetu*) for inference according to valid cognition;

for inference proceeds by way of identity (*tādātmya*), causality (*tadutpatti*), or concomitance (*samanvaya*), and its operation is observed only with respect to a property (*dharma*) as qualified by another property.
Therefore, since [the object] is qualified by the property (*dharma*), verbal cognition would not be inference, but would be like perception.
Since such objects are excluded by virtue of lacking the three characteristics [of a valid logical reason],
how could there be any effort toward establishing that word as inference?
Ms.
An object of a different nature has already been established; for it will be demonstrated that both word and logical mark have the universal as their object, and this applies to the word as well.

"The subject (dharmin) and that which possesses the property as its qualifier (dharmaviśiṣṭa) are the bearer of the mark (liṅgin); this has been established. In this manuscript, the word "dharma" appears with a blurred or uncertain reading.
When the object, the locus, and the word are established therein, the probandum is proven.

For it is never accepted that a subject (*dharmin*) which is already established can be something to be proven (*sādhya*). If, on the other hand, it is the object (*artha*) that is to be proven and not the sound (*dhvani*), then why is the word itself not postulated as the subject (*pakṣa*) by virtue of its possessing the object?
For in that case, it would follow that the reason is merely a part of the meaning of the thesis;
indeed, a universal is accepted as the reason with respect to a specific property-possessor (dharmin) within the subject (pakṣa).
Here, "soundness" (śabdatva) is the indicator, and not "the state of being the word 'cow'" (gośabdatva) that serves as the logical mark (liṅga).

For there is no establishment of a relationship with that [past object]; even if it were established, inference would be useless. Or, if that object is sought to be proven as being connected by way of existing at another time, the persistence of Śrīharṣa and others through that other time is never established.
Alternatively, if the state of being accomplished through the meaning of a sentence is not [known] by one who knows the connection with the meaning of the sentence,
how can its status as inference be established beforehand?
For in that case, the establishment of the prior object arises from the sentence itself.
In this way, it is not established in reality that a sentence is merely a form of inference;
for apart from words, nothing called a "sentence" can be defined.
Regarding the statement: "In the case of sentence-meaning, there is no inference regarding the meanings of individual words; how then can there be the status of sentence-meaning therein? (Ms.)
In that context, the existence of the word's property of being a predicate (pakṣadharmatva) is thus established here;
for nowhere is there a relation [of a word] apart from the relation between an action and its agent.
The king is the supporter of man; therefore he is called "rājā" (the king), and by that [support] he is called the king's [property],
*rājya*.
The tree stands; those branches belong to it, or they are there in it.

In a location possessing fire, smoke possesses the status of an agent with respect to its coming into being; because of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and so forth, action (*kriyā*) exists everywhere.
Furthermore, no relation is accepted that has an unapprehended form, nor is there any relation whose form is not cognized.

And since it does not exist in what is non-existent, nor can there be a genitive tatpuruṣa compound with that which is non-existent, it cannot be determined that this is a property of the subject (pakṣadharma).
Ms.
Therefore, in this case,
the positive concomitance (anvaya) of the word with the object of cognition is also established.
For it is through the operation of the suffix *an* that the status of being a connector (*anvetṛtva*) is perceived for all [words]. (Ms.)
In the case of smoke, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is clear, in that wherever smoke exists, fire exists; however,
there is no such certainty that wherever a word exists, its object exists.
If it is argued that [the mind] would be eternal because of its omnipresence, and thus equal with respect to all objects;
Ms.
reads "nityavitutvā".
Because by that [means] everything has been seen, or because the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is understood. (Ms.: because it has been seen).
It would follow that all words convey every object without exception.
Furthermore, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) of a word never has an object as its domain.

If it is argued that there is no certainty regarding the non-existence of words when their objects do not exist, because [the object] is not perceived, we reply: this understanding is not always present;
thus, the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) stated by the opponent is not tenable.
For comprehension for the sake of cultivation arises precisely from convention.
All comprehension of word-meanings occurs nowhere without convention; if that convention is the manifestor, it is not perceived otherwise [than as such].
For in the case of a manifesting corpse,
no contrary connection is ever manifested through convention.
In some cases,
what was not established through direct perception is established otherwise at another time.
For it is not logical that there be a cognition of an object through direct perception in that case;
otherwise, if the convention were different, how could there be a connection with another object?
If there were manifold meanings everywhere, cognition would become confused; for cognition [is indeed...]
Nor is there ever any cognition of the true nature of a thing from that [conceptualization], for everyone acts here and there by means of this [conceptualization] through the force of desire.
In the case of identity, every fault that arises from the relation of everything with everything has already been shown;
furthermore, the manifestation of a relation is precisely what constitutes the statement of that relation.
In that which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), the meaningfulness of the statement is not ascertained through verbal communication;
nor is a person who teaches it perceived as an authoritative source (*pramāṇa*).
[Objection: This relationship is beginningless, and thus it is a continuous tradition (*sāṃtānaparamparā*). [Response: That is indeed a continuous tradition.
And since the referents of the words are not established, how can there be truth in the meaning of the sentence?
Nevertheless, there may be a perversion of the meanings of words arising from humans;
but since there is no human author in the Veda, how could there be an act of perversion? For perversion is indeed observed when the intention of humans is corrupted.
There is no human author of the Veda; how could there be such a misconception?
Indeed, there is no human [author] of the Veda.
If it is argued that this is a misconception, here too another response is stated by others who hold a different view.
Just as error is not possible here without a person,
and thus non-error there is intrinsic and not due to a cause,
so too error there is intrinsic and likewise without a cause.
Even in the Veda, a misconception regarding the nature of things is observed;
for therein, entities such as the self and space are indeed unreal.
Even though an object is real, one engages in worldly discourse by saying, "Do this"; thus,
an object perceived through another means of valid cognition is recognized in various contexts.
Therefore, having ascertained its meaning, the wise proceed to act;

but since the Veda lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how can one proceed here? If it is argued that the Veda itself is the authority (*māna*) in that regard, it has no established validity.
Moreover, if the awakening to the meaning arises from the Veda,
why does it not also arise from what is not the Veda? Or what is the distinction in that case?
Is there no awakening, or is conceptual construction not a revealer of objects not previously perceived?
To claim that such an object exists merely on the basis of postulating the unseen (adṛṣṭa) is extreme audacity; yet,
if that object is indeed ascertained, then it possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
Certainty does not arise for everyone from that very [source]; rather, it arises only from the certainty of some.
If validity were based solely on certainty, then all [cognitions] would be valid;
or else, the validity of certainty would derive from the fact that the sentence is of non-human origin.
But in the case of the Veda, it is restricted in this way precisely by means of human speech.
Ms.
pauruṣeyā tu.
For even from that which is not of human origin, the meaning is not understood in this way;
rather, it is from the Veda itself that the cognition of the conceptualized meaning arises— this is the knowledge of reality.
Because the meaning is explained separately for the sake of conceptual differentiation, the meaning is not perceived from the Veda in some instances.
Ms.
In this very way it has been explained by me elsewhere; such is the established rule.
However, through even slight practice, certainty is attained in all cases.
There is the observation of the meaning of such sentences as "Ms., bring Devadatta," and so forth.

Furthermore, if there is no arising of perceptual cognition regarding the meaning of a sentence, then that meaning is accessible solely through the sentence; this being the case, one who knows [the meaning] would not be a "yogin" (one possessing direct knowledge).
Consequently, how could there be a grasping of the relationship between the sentence and its meaning?
If the comprehension of the sentence-meaning occurs through the understanding of the relationship between the meanings of the words within the sentence and the non-sentence;
There exists for it a relation—even though unreal—such as that with fruits on a riverbank and so forth.
Ms.
There exists for it a relation—even though unreal.
Or rather, one should assume the reading "for here there is a connection, even if it is unreal," out of fear of breaking the meter;
for what proof is there that it exists there due to its association with *nara*, yet does not exist here?
Furthermore, regarding the Narayana-sacrifice, since there is no Puruṣa [author] there, that [sacrifice] does not exist either; what proof is there for it?
And to claim that there is a connection there without a Puruṣa is mere audacity.
If there is gain from that [connection], why is it not accepted even for what is meaningless?
Just as there is no relationship [between them], so too there is no lack of relationship.
Furthermore, what is the purpose of establishing a convention if there is no connection with a denotable object?
Lady Saṅgati:
Is it then that when he exists, the intended meaning becomes possible?
If it were otherwise, the employment of a word would not be devoid of meaning; since it is never the case that it is devoid of meaning— because meaning is possible in every instance—
the referent of a word always exists, and it is held that the universal (*sāmānya*) is the denoted object.
And if the meaning of a word were the universal (sāmānya), there would be no deviation [of the word from its object];
yet this is not the case, because when the relationship of signifier and signified is not accepted in this way,
doubt as to "how," "from what," or "where" remains unresolved.
If it is argued that there is no doubt whatsoever regarding the generality [of the object] in the form "Where?", then where would that doubt arise?
If it is argued that the particular is not [identical to] the universal alone, [we reply: why? Because the former depends upon the latter.
From the meaning itself there is doubt; from the word, there is certainty regarding its own referent. (The reading "svārtho viniścayaḥ" is preferred.)
But surely a sentence that produces doubt regarding its meaning would not be inciting;
for, like individual words, it would lack denotative power due to universal doubt.
Indeed, in a sentence such as "Devadatta," there is a collection of the meanings of those constituent words.
One who understands doubt would think that [the cognition] depends on its own causes and so forth;
however, because of the statement "there is no doubt regarding what is intended," there is engagement [with the object].
Ms.
In a case of doubt,
a word becomes non-expressive because there is no ascertainment of the intended meaning; moreover, the cognition of a universal is a failure when there is no connection with the individual instance.
Furthermore, there is no apprehension of a universal that is inseparable from the individual; nor does a universal ever appear when there is an appearance of color and shape.
And that [which appears] is not the universal, because it is apprehended as being excluded [from others].
For there is no cognition of one thing when another color and shape are being perceived;
therefore, it is only when there is doubt regarding a particular that a universal is observed.
If there is doubt regarding it, or if it causes doubt, how can its non-ambiguous nature be asserted?
Consequently, the sentence is non-expressive; how, then, can it possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)?
And the categories of existence, such as the self and so forth, are seen only for the sake of their passing away (or, according to the manuscript reading:
only for the sake of their separation).
If, in reality, there exists a prior [state] consisting in being authorless (apauruṣeya), then...
By what means is it understood that there is no connection with a contrary object?
Just as falsity arises from a person, so too would truthfulness arise from a person;
thus, a connection that is entirely independent [of a person] is not observed anywhere.

How is it that what is seen in the sentence "Fire [is] the enemy of cold" does not attain the status of reality, even though it is seen? This is not the actual meaning of the word, just like the words "Bharata" and "araṇi."

For the determination of the meaning of a sentence would indeed depend upon the determination of the meanings of its constituent words; or, if the meanings of the words are not real, is that which is perceived [in the sentence] itself the sentence-meaning?
It is merely imagined, since it is seen only by human beings.
In the speech of a madman, there is never any truth in the connection [of words]. (Ms.: *unmatte*)
The wise imagine some [connection] by virtue of their own corresponding influence;
however, he does not perceive a connection between words.
Even in the Veda there is no perception of such a connection; here too, there is a lack of truth.
When there is no relation because of its non-existence even in the Veda due to its being the product of a madman, then there can be no perception of such a relation therein.
In the case of that which is not of human origin, the cognition of the relationship is all the more impossible;
if the relationship were inherent, why is it not postulated for the Veda as well?
Ms.
If it is argued that there is no connection [of authorship] there, then how could that [connection] exist even in the Veda?
Therefore, this [connection] is not found either in the words of a madman or in the Veda.
It is established that "attaining" (āsādya) and "achieving" (āpādya) by men are both equal. (The manuscript reads *samadvayam*.)

Therefore, there is no cognition of an object from a word by way of an invariable connection (pratibandha), just as there is none from the word "pratīpa" [and its synonyms]. Nor is there a perceptual cognition of the object;
for how can it be understood that there is a cognition of something that is not perceived?
Furthermore, no entity whatsoever is observed without a convention.
Alternatively, the reading may be *kalpistu*,
or even *kalpitastu* is possible;
in that case, the connection of meaning previously observed would be joined with another word-meaning.
Because words are related to other words, this [cognition] is likewise [conceptual] even in this case;
therefore, this is merely inference proceeding toward an object that is not external.
Consequently, the authority of words also resides only in an object established by the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*).
Since it is similar to that [convention], the Veda also possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding external objects;
this relationship is beginningless, and thus it is not a mere circularity. Furthermore, in the absence of comprehension, the relationship cannot be established.
The validity [of scripture] is established through the comprehension of meaning; it is not established with respect to an external object.
In the case of the Veda, that [validity] does not arise from the meaning, for it is like the letters bored by a woodworm (*ghuṇākṣara*);
moreover, no definite limit exists anywhere among those woodworm letters.
Therefore, even in that case, let authorship by a person be accepted;
just as there is no [arbitrary] letter-carving by wood-boring insects (ghuṇākṣara), so too there is no lack of authorship.
For how could even that which is not authored by a person be like the manifold world of conceptual proliferation?
Therefore, let it be understood that this Veda is merely a human fabrication;
for there is no proof of any excellence in a person [who composed it], nor is there any authority in that [Veda].
Furthermore, the object [of cognition] in that case is of a different nature than what has been stated regarding the inferential mark (liṅga) and the word (śabda).
Therefore, the lack of validity in verbal testimony is established in every respect;

for it has been proven that the object of a word is indeed conceptual construction (vikalpa). Furthermore, it has been stated that according to inference, the subject (dharmin) as qualified by its property (dharma) is the probandum (sādhya).
If sound were not a property of the subject (pakṣadharma), it would lack the status of a logical reason (hetu) regarding an external object;

for when the locus (dharmin) is unestablished, an object such as smoke cannot be proven. Indeed, it is precisely because of its connection with the locus that even perception possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Nor is there the state of being a basis, nor indeed is there the establishment of perception (pratyakṣa).
Ms.
nicā.
It is not even conceivable that there is a basis [for this], as it would result in a logical fallacy.
By what reasoning could even perception be considered an inference? Or rather, how will it be conceptualized?
Furthermore, if the three-fold character [of a logical mark] is absent, perception cannot be established as perception itself when it is devoid of the nature of inference,
even if one imagines that the word is the subject (pakṣa) by virtue of its possessing meaning.
The consequence of being a part of the meaning of the thesis does not apply to the nature of sound.
The word is proven [to be eternal], for it is a word by virtue of being a word, just like a previous word.
Just as smoke, being connected in the sense of proximity, [is known] by its nature as smoke; such is the connection.
If the property of being the word "go" (cow) is unestablished [in the case] of those words denoting creepers, palmyra trees, and so forth;
[if it is argued that] the word "go" itself is unestablished.
The establishment [of the meaning] would be for the sake of a specific distinction; therefore, the state of being specific is logical,
for for us the connection of the sentence-meaning with the general sense is already established.
Furthermore, there is no specific relationship [between the word and its object] established anywhere;
thus, it is inconsistent to claim that the sentence itself possesses the nature of inference.
A word that establishes a relationship is called a sentence (vākya).
Relationship (saṃbandha).
The whole is the subject (dharmin), while a part is the reason (hetu).
Ms.
[states]: "by means of the reason."
And why is it that the relation itself does not possess the status of the probandum (*sādhya*)?
How could there be a "relating" (*saṃbandhana*) apart from the relation between an action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*)? [For example:
"The king is the supporter of the man," or "the word is the filler of the sentence."
A tree stands upon its branches; why then does a word not likewise stand upon its sentence?
Just as fire possesses agency with respect to smoke in a smoky place, so it is for the root *bhū*.
Just as it occurs for you and as it exists for you,
so too is it examined whether there is not likewise [the same status] for a word within a sentence.
[Objection: Let it be examined; for a relation whose form is not cognized is not perceived either.
Nor does there exist a relation [of identity] with that; for if a relation were present, there would also be a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound.

Consequently, this property of the subject (pakṣadharma) is established by the word itself, like other words; yet there is no positive concomitance (anvaya) of the word [with its object], and so forth—this is the proof of what is already established.
There is no positive concomitance with an external object anywhere, for a word is observed even without an object.
If it is argued that [the self] is perceived because of its eternal omnipresence, then such a concomitance would likewise exist with respect to all objects.
Then, O Lady Bhavonitya, in the state of the accomplishment of all aims, upon the convergence of all sounds.
When the relationship between the signified and the signifier has been stated,
that [relationship] is indeed a further succession.
It has been demonstrated that there is also no negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) for a word,
because even one who understands [the meaning] otherwise may intend to speak otherwise; therefore,
there is absolutely no way to ascertain the cognitions of others from the words of a person.
The feminine [form] is used after a word that has a masculine form.
The movement of the intellect belongs to one who is deluded; furthermore, when there is a desire to express one thing, another sentence is observed [to be uttered].
Ms.
For one who is deluded,
[action] proceeds according to whatever is intended; therefore, it does not proceed at all when non-delusion is fully known through the cultivation of conceptualization and so forth.
Due to repeated practice and conceptualization,
when there is simultaneity, the intended meaning is understood.
The worldly convention is established in this very manner;
otherwise, it has been proven that everything would lack validity.
Without such convention, there is no one who partakes in birth, even in the world of Brahmā.
Thus, that which is attached to the meaning, established by worldly usage, and verbal, is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of inference with respect to its own object.
Ms.
*ityarthasi* [is corrected to *ityarthasaṅgi*].

But externally, there is no other means of valid cognition for this [scripture] whatsoever; however, insofar as the existence of the world is established here in some manner, verbal testimony is included within the means of valid cognition. Thus ends the first chapter on the inclusion of verbal testimony within the means of valid cognition.
Now begins the second chapter.
Even comparison (upamā) is accepted as a means of valid cognition (pramā) by some of those with clear intelligence.
The determination of an imperceptible object occurs through similarity; without that [similarity],
it is impossible to deny the reality of similarity itself.
Furthermore, the application of a commonality of parts cannot serve to invalidate [the distinction], for that [application] belongs to a different class; moreover,
analogy is observed as a means of cognition regarding similarity when the object is beyond the senses.
The definition of inference does not apply there, because first there is the apprehension of similarity;
therefore, that which is remembered must be qualified by its similarity [to the perceived object].
Even though the object of knowledge— namely, the specific excellence characterized by similarity to that [cow], or the similarity itself as inhering in it—
has been perceived by direct perception and subsequently remembered in the cow through that similarity, [it remains that the relation is not previously known].
Since the specific [object] is not established through any other means, it is the authority of analogy (*upamāna*),
